Bowman, Supervisory Modernization After Silicon Valley Bank
headlines.officialText: Frontline examiners, risk and surveillance specialists, and Reserve Bank and Board staff knew about SVB's exposure to interest rate and liquidity risk at least as early as nine full months before the Federal Deposit Insurance Corporation took the bank into receivership. The preliminary review also corrects earlier mischaracterization that social media was to blame for the run on SVB, and that the Fed's failure to act was caused by statutory tailoring or regulatory changes.2 Instead, the report notes long-standing problems in supervisory accountability and decisionmaking as the most significant contributors to the failure to issue timely critical enforcement actions related to core risks. The review notes that supervisory attention at SVB often centered on process, procedure, governance, and controls rather than on mitigating the underlying interest rate and liquidity exposures. SVB had 54 matters requiring attention or immediate attention between 2019 and the time of its failure, yet none of those supervisory findings required the bank to address its core financial risks. In other words, a supervisory organization can be extremely busy and still fail to focus sufficiently on the risks that matter most. In our structure, different groups identified risks, many others were expected to concur, and yet no individual clearly owned the obligation to reach a decision and propel action. Modern supervisory organizations increasingly rely on surveillance, specialist teams, and data analysis that allow us to identify patterns across institutions. They refocus supervisory efforts on what matters most: early identification of material risks, exercising sound supervisory judgment, and a broad range of supervisory tools to enable timely and proportionate action to address material risks before they threaten the safety and soundness of an institution or the stability of the financial system. This includes concentrating on material risks, appropriately tailoring supervisory intensity, periodically reconsidering processes that may have accumulated over time to ensure they are still fit for purpose, and providing clarity so that supervisors can reach decisions quickly enough to make a difference. It means directing supervisory attention to the risks that are most material given the institution's size, complexity, activities, business model, interconnectedness, and potential impact on financial stability. A supervisory organization that treats every issue as equally important will tend to devote substantial attention to matters that are easiest to document, measure, and track, leaving other risks that require synthesis, experience, and enhanced judgment to receive less attention than they deserve. It should be to identify the risks that matter most and address them while there is still time to alter the trajectory. The independent review determined that these reports from the BCBS and the FSB generally repeated existing claims by other reports rather than independently verifying the information or increasing the breadth of evidence offered in their support. The BCBS's mandate is to strengthen regulation and supervision practices worldwide with the purpose of enhancing financial stability.3 Similarly, the FSB was established to coordinate and promote effective regulatory, supervisory, and other financial-sector policies in the interest of global financial stability.4 To maintain their credibility, these institutions must redouble their focus on material risks—those that affect safety and soundness or financial stability—while eschewing less valuable work that misdirects resources toward less valuable priorities. Simply accepting data and analysis without rigorous validation risks building international standards on flawed foundations, potentially undermining both the effectiveness of regulations and the credibility of these critical institutions. For instance, how do we organize our people to allocate authority and prioritize risks? A critical measure of whether that modernization succeeds will be whether supervisors are able to identify the risks that matter and act decisively at the point when their actions can have the greatest impact.
